extracted.intended_audience: general readers; journalists; human-rights advocates; legal practitioners and scholars interested in comparative defamation law
extracted.subtask_description: A comparative, global overview of legal, social, and religious standards that define, limit, or punish defamation (libel, slander, insult, blasphemy), and related procedural and remedial practices. Covers statutory elements, defenses, trends (decriminalization/extension online), intermediary liability, and religious/ethical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thai criminal defamation (Section 326)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever imputes anything to the other person before a third person in a manner likely to impair the reputation of such other person or to expose such other person to be hated or scorned, is said to commit defamation, and shall be punished with imprisonment not exceeding one year or fined not exceeding twenty thousand Baht, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 327 extends to defamation to the family: imputing something about a deceased person that is likely to impair reputation of father, mother, spouse or child of the deceased is punished as under Section 326.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition categories: libel, slander, insult, lese-majesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation law covers various exercises of expression (criminal libel, defamation, slander, insult, and lese‑majesty) depending on jurisdictional terminology and scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different jurisdictions use different labels and may combine or separate these concepts; civil vs criminal treatment varies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as a defense (jurisdiction-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many common-law jurisdictions the truth of an allegation can be a defense in civil libel cases; historically truth was irrelevant in criminal libel because it was considered an offence against the public rather than solely the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 6 of the Libel Act 1843 allowed truth as a defense in criminal libel only if publication was for the 'public benefit'. Modern application varies widely; U.S. First Amendment law and state/federal rules shape availability of truth as a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest / public benefit defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication may be defensible if it can be shown it was for the public benefit or public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically required in some criminal libel defences (e.g., Libel Act 1843). Modern statutes and case law may recognize public interest as a defense to defamation (explicitly noted in at least 21 countries as of one report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof (often on defendant)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many jurisdictions the burden of proof in defamation proceedings rests on the defendant, making it difficult for publishers to prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes that in many African states and other jurisdictions burden of proof continued to be on the defendant and public interest was rarely recognized as a defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal vs civil remedies and trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation may be prosecuted criminally or pursued civilly for damages; there has been a trend toward using civil defamation in lieu of criminal prosecution, but with often disproportionate fines and damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil suits can be used to bankrupt media outlets; some countries have decriminalized defamation while civil claims remain robust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decriminalization recommendations and international standards
rubrics_metrics.description: International bodies (UNESCO, OSCE, regional human rights bodies) have campaigned for decriminalization or reform of defamation laws to align with freedom of expression standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UNESCO provided technical assistance on revising legislation; OSCE had an ongoing decriminalization campaign; regional bodies have issued resolutions urging repeal of criminal defamation and insult laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of defamation laws to silence journalists and critics
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation laws are frequently used to censor journalists and activists critical of governments, sometimes leading to arrest, imprisonment, suspension of outlets, or heavy fines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples across regions include imprisonment of bloggers and journalists, trials in military courts in some post‑Arab Spring contexts, and use of anti‑state or terrorism charges instead of or alongside defamation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel tourism / forum shopping
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful individuals have shopped around for jurisdictions most likely to approve their defamation suits, thereby limiting critical and dissenting voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Known as 'libel tourism'; international reforms (e.g., SPEECH Act in U.S.) and domestic law changes aim to limit enforceability of offshore judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of defamation laws to online content
rubrics_metrics.description: Many countries have extended criminal and civil defamation provisions to online content, leading to prosecutions and other controls over bloggers and social media users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cybercrime and anti‑terrorism laws have been used to target online speech; technological advances enable states to monitor online content more effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediary / ISP liability and privatized censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Private internet intermediaries (platforms, ISPs) may be held liable for user-generated content, creating incentives for over‑compliance with takedown requests and preventive censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include excessive content removal outside legal process, lack of recourse for content producers, inadequate due process and judicial oversight, and opaque blocking/filtering processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content removal requests and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments make content removal requests to platforms citing defamation, privacy, security, etc.; transparency of rationale and processes varies by platform and jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform transparency reports (Google, Meta, Twitter) show rising numbers of government requests. Only some platforms publish rationales; lack of transparency undermines accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPEECH Act and protection from foreign libel judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. federal law (SPEECH Act) and state laws (e.g., New York's Rachel's Law) limit enforceability of offshore libel judgments that do not comply with U.S. First Amendment standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These laws were passed to shield American writers and publishers from foreign judgments inconsistent with U.S. free‑speech protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague language and disproportionate punishments threaten free expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws and regulations adopting vague definitions of defamation or imposing disproportionate penalties threaten online freedom of expression and press freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports noted dozens of post‑2016 laws and amendments with vague language or harsh punishments across many countries; such provisions facilitate censorship and chilling effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation of religion / blasphemy laws intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: Many countries have laws penalizing blasphemy, apostasy, or defamation of religion; these interact with defamation law and freedom of expression concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UN and regional bodies have debated and issued guidance (Rabat Plan of Action); a substantial number of states retain such laws, sometimes combined with hate‑speech rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential protection for public officials and heads of state
rubrics_metrics.description: Some laws provide greater protection or harsher punishments when defamation involves public officials, state bodies, or heads of state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This increased protection has been noted in several regions and can limit scrutiny of government actions; European Court of Human Rights decisions have influenced reforms unevenly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of other offences (terrorism, anti‑state, emergency laws) to punish speech
rubrics_metrics.description: States may use broadly framed offences (terrorism, incitement, national security) or emergency measures to suppress speech that elsewhere would be treated as defamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This trend was noted in multiple regions where defamation charges are complemented or replaced by other criminal offences to silence dissent.

rubrics_metrics.name: SLAPPs (strategic lawsuits against public participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil defamation suits can be used strategically to silence critics, journalists, and public participation by imposing costly litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rise of internet publication has contributed to increased SLAPPs; some jurisdictions have statutory defenses or expedited dismissal mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional / case law drivers of reform (court rulings and precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Court decisions at national and regional levels (e.g., African Court, national constitutional courts) can overturn convictions and prompt legal reform toward decriminalization or reduced penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Lohé Issa Konaté v. Burkina Faso (African Court) and constitutional court rulings in Zimbabwe and Kenya that declared criminal defamation provisions unconstitutional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed non‑criminal remedies and procedural reforms (example: Malaysian proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals to harmonize defamation law with human‑rights or religious principles include non‑criminal remedies (right of reply, orders of retraction, mediation, ombudsman, empowerment of human rights bodies), limits on monetary awards, and education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Malaysian academic proposal also suggested categorizing defamatory acts and prescribing a mix of hadd/tazir/monetary punishments under certain interpretations of Islamic law, while recommending institutional mechanisms for dispute resolution and public education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/ethical categorizations: Catholic teaching on defamation, detraction, and slander
rubrics_metrics.description: Catholic moral teaching forbids lies, detraction, calumny and slander; degree of sinfulness depends on harm done, criminality of the allegation, trustworthiness of the detractor, and dignity of the victim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions may exist (for the good of the guilty or to prevent a greater evil) and remedies emphasize restraint, fraternal correction, reparation, and restitution; journalists and historians are afforded some latitude for public interest reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/ethical categorizations: Jewish law (calumny / lashon hara / slander)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jewish tradition distinguishes lashon hara (true but harmful speech / detraction) from slander (false and malicious defamation); both are morally condemned, with severe social and religious sanctions described in rabbinic literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal remedies historically included fines, atonement, restitution and sometimes excommunication; the literature emphasizes the moral gravity of injuring another's reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/ethical categorizations: Islamic perspectives and proposed legal harmonization
rubrics_metrics.description: Islamic definitions as discussed in an academic Malaysian paper encompass mislead, accuse of adultery, embarrass or discredit dignity/honour; the author proposed harmonizing Malaysian laws with Islamic principles, enumerating defamation types (libel, slander, adultery/sodomy, acts against honour) and proposing three punishment types (criminal hadd, criminal tazir, monetary damages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposal also suggested institutional reforms (right of reply, retraction, mediation, ombudsman, empowerment of Human Rights Commission, education) and that reforms be consistent with constitutional provisions recognizing Islam as state religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies of retraction, restitution and reparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Across legal and religious frameworks, remedies for defamation can include retraction orders, restitution, compensation (damages/fines), and reputational restoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious texts emphasize retraction and restitution as moral remedies; some legal reforms recommend procedural remedies (right of reply, mediation) instead of or alongside criminal penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform / state interplay and lack of due process in takedowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Privatized censorship arises where platforms remove or block content in response to state requests without adequate legal process, judicial oversight, or transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns highlighted include widening ranges of content deemed harmful, inadequate judicial oversight, lack of transparency around blocking/filtering processes, and the exchange of personal data between states and private companies.
